paragraphs: This paper tackles the overlap between two difficult requirements: learning an image classification task from very few examples and resisting adversarial examples. Previous approaches to robust classification typically require large training sets and expensive training procedures. Few-shot methods address the shortage of examples, but the authors identify their vulnerability to adversarial inputs as a substantial obstacle.

The proposed algorithm, Adversarial Querying, aims to produce robust meta-learners. The learning objective therefore concerns a model’s ability to handle new classification tasks with little data while also maintaining robustness. The paper pairs this algorithmic contribution with an investigation into the causes of adversarial vulnerability, connecting the proposed approach to the problem it is intended to address.

On few-shot image classification tasks including Mini-ImageNet and CIFAR-FS, the authors report substantially stronger robust performance than robust transfer learning. These findings support meta-learning as a useful route toward combining limited-data adaptation with adversarial robustness in the evaluated settings. The contribution is the combination of those capabilities within a single learning approach.
neurips-2020-adversarially-robust-few-sh.tldr: Adversarial Querying trains meta-learners that achieve substantially stronger adversarial robustness than robust transfer learning on evaluated few-shot classification tasks.

paragraphs: Score matching offers a way to train energy-based models without calculating the partition function, a normalization quantity that can be difficult to compute. Extending this advantage to models with hidden variables has largely remained unresolved beyond special cases. This paper proposes Bi-level Score Matching, or BiSM, to make score matching applicable to latent-variable models with more general structures.

BiSM rewrites training as two connected optimization problems. The higher level introduces an approximate posterior distribution over hidden variables and optimizes a modified score-matching objective. The lower level improves that approximation by fitting it to the true posterior. A stochastic algorithm uses gradient unrolling to account for this nested optimization, and the authors analyze both the method’s consistency and the algorithm’s convergence.

Experiments cover Gaussian restricted Boltzmann machines and complex models built with deep convolutional networks. BiSM performs comparably to contrastive divergence and ordinary score matching where those methods apply. It also trains models with intractable posteriors to generate natural images, demonstrating the promise of extending score matching to a broader model class.
neurips-2020-bi-level-score-matching-for.tldr: BiSM uses nested optimization to extend score matching to general energy-based latent-variable models, including models with intractable posteriors.

paragraphs: Langevin dynamics uses randomness to explore a non-convex objective, finding local minima and eventually visiting a global minimum over longer timescales. Its usual diffusion is reversible in time. This paper studies whether breaking that property improves optimization, examining underdamped Langevin dynamics and a variant with a non-symmetric drift.

For a specified local minimum, the authors establish a high-probability alternative. By a recurrence time, a trajectory either ends outside a small neighborhood of that minimum or enters the neighborhood and remains for a potentially exponentially long escape time. For the underdamped method, the recurrence-time bound improves on ordinary Langevin dynamics in its dependence on the smallest Hessian eigenvalue at the minimum. They obtain similar improvements for the non-symmetric-drift method.

The paper also analyzes discrete-time escape when an objective has two local minima separated by a saddle point. In that setting, the non-reversible variants can leave a basin of attraction faster, with quantified improvements. Together, these results suggest advantages both for locating local minima and for exploring beyond them.
neurips-2020-breaking-reversibility-acce.tldr: Two non-reversible Langevin variants improve theoretical recurrence-time bounds and can escape local basins faster in an analyzed two-minimum setting.

paragraphs: Vision-language grounding connects a sentence to a particular image region or video moment. In the weakly supervised setting studied here, training supplies sentences for whole images or videos without directly identifying the relevant region or moment. This makes learning precise alignment difficult. Existing approaches either rely heavily on randomly chosen negative examples or cannot directly optimize the visual-textual alignment score.

The authors propose Counterfactual Contrastive Learning to create informative comparisons through deliberate transformations. Robust and destructive transformations produce counterfactual positive and negative results for contrastive training. This gives the learning process comparisons based on controlled changes to the information involved in grounding, addressing weaknesses in the existing training paradigms.

The transformations operate at three levels. They damage visual features of selected proposals, confuse interactions between language and vision, or destroy contextual clues in relationships among proposals. Experiments on five grounding datasets support the approach’s effectiveness. The findings indicate that constructing contrasts around these different information sources can help learn localization from annotations that only describe the overall image or video.
neurips-2020-counterfactual-contrastive-.tldr: Counterfactual Contrastive Learning improves weakly supervised grounding by constructing contrasts through changes to visual features, cross-modal interactions, and proposal relationships.

paragraphs: One-shot architecture search saves training effort by letting candidate networks share weights inside a larger hypernetwork. A drawback is that individual subnetworks can receive insufficient training, weakening the candidates being considered. This paper introduces architecture distillation to improve their training through collaboration among subnetworks.

The method maintains prioritized paths: candidate architectures that perform well during training. These candidates teach other subnetworks by transferring knowledge, with the aim of improving individual convergence. The prioritized set changes as candidate performance and complexity change. At the end, the method selects the most promising prioritized path directly, avoiding an additional search procedure based on reinforcement learning or evolutionary algorithms.

ImageNet experiments show improvements in hypernetwork convergence and performance as well as subnetwork training. Under aligned settings, the discovered architectures outperform the compared MobileNetV3 and EfficientNet families. Experiments on object detection and a more challenging search space further support the method’s generality and robustness. The results suggest that improving how shared-weight candidates learn can benefit both architecture selection and the resulting models.
neurips-2020-cream-of-the-crop-distillin.tldr: Distilling knowledge from dynamically prioritized subnetworks improves one-shot architecture search and enables direct selection of a strong final architecture.

paragraphs: DiffGCN develops graph convolution, pooling, and unpooling operations for unordered data such as point clouds and meshes. Its central idea is to borrow mathematical tools from finite differences and algebraic multigrid. These frameworks supply a way to describe local operations and hierarchical representations even when inputs do not lie on a regular image grid.

The convolution kernel is parameterized through discretized differential operators using graph mass, gradient, and Laplacian quantities. Consequently, its parameterization follows the meaning of those operators rather than depending on a particular graph structure. Pooling and unpooling draw on algebraic multigrid methods, which are used to solve partial differential equations on unstructured grids, to support representations at multiple levels.

The authors explain the construction by relating it to standard convolutional networks on regular grids. Experiments including classification and part segmentation achieve results comparable to or better than the state of the art, and the paper analyzes computational costs relative to other graph networks. These findings support differential operators and multigrid ideas as useful foundations for learning on irregular data.
neurips-2020-diffgcn-graph-convolutional.tldr: DiffGCN builds graph convolutions from differential operators and hierarchical pooling from algebraic multigrid, achieving competitive classification and segmentation results.

paragraphs: Directed graphs carry information in the orientation of their connections. Converting them to undirected graphs so that a graph Laplacian becomes symmetric can discard this information and distort the weights used in message passing. The paper also identifies a separate problem: a fixed receptive field in each graph convolution layer limits the collection of features at different scales.

The authors extend spectral graph convolution theoretically to directed graphs and derive a simplified form using personalized PageRank. Their Digraph Inception Convolutional Network, or DiGCN, combines directed convolution with higher-order proximity. This lets the network use larger receptive fields and learn from graph relationships at multiple scales while retaining directed structure.

Experiments indicate that DiGCN captures more structural information from directed graphs than conventional GCNs. The authors also report improvements when their approach is extended to other models and superior performance against state-of-the-art methods across the evaluated benchmarks. The contribution connects a directed spectral formulation with an architecture designed to use both direction and scale as sources of information.
neurips-2020-digraph-inception-convoluti.tldr: DiGCN extends spectral convolution to directed graphs and combines multiple neighborhood scales to improve structural representations and benchmark performance.

paragraphs: This paper introduces Direct Policy Gradient algorithms for reinforcement learning with discrete actions. The approach combines direct optimization, which approximates gradients by optimizing a random objective, with A* sampling, which supports that optimization over large spaces. The resulting method finds trajectories that optimize a random objective and uses them to approximate a policy gradient.

A practical benefit is the ability to incorporate domain knowledge during training through upper bounds on return-to-go. Such bounds play a role similar to guidance in heuristic search while the algorithm still computes a policy-gradient approximation. This connects structured search over possible trajectories with the learning process used to improve the policy.

The analysis identifies cases where DirPG has an exponentially higher probability of obtaining informative gradients than REINFORCE. It also reveals built-in variance reduction and interprets a parameter previously treated as a numerical approximation as controlling risk sensitivity. Experiments examine key design choices and show good performance against baselines in illustrative domains. The exponential advantage is therefore a result for particular cases, alongside supporting empirical examples.
neurips-2020-direct-policy-gradients-dir.tldr: DirPG approximates policy gradients through randomized trajectory optimization, allowing search bounds and offering more informative gradients in some analyzed cases.

paragraphs: Distributed second-order optimization uses information from worker machines to update a model at a central machine. Communication can become a significant part of that process, and Byzantine worker failures introduce unreliable contributions. This paper develops an approximate Newton-type algorithm that addresses communication efficiency and resilience to those failures together.

Workers communicate with the central machine only once per iteration. The compared methods, GIANT and DINGO, require two sequential communications involving local gradient and Hessian information. The proposed algorithm also uses a simple threshold based on norms to filter Byzantine workers, incorporating a robustness mechanism into the distributed optimization procedure.

The authors establish a linear-quadratic convergence rate and show that communication savings and Byzantine resilience incur only a small statistical error rate for arbitrary convex loss functions. Experiments on synthetic data and a benchmark LIBSVM dataset support the theoretical analysis. The contribution demonstrates that reducing communication and handling faulty workers can be combined within a second-order method while retaining the stated convergence behavior and statistical accuracy.
neurips-2020-distributed-newton-can-comm.tldr: An approximate distributed Newton method combines one communication per iteration with Byzantine-worker filtering and theoretical convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: A population of reinforcement learning agents can explore through different behaviors, increasing the range of experience available for learning. However, encouraging diversity with pairwise distances can lead to cycling and redundant behavior. Explicit diversity rewards can also interfere with refining behaviors that already earn good rewards, leaving the balance between exploration and reward dependent on heuristics.

Diversity via Determinants, or DvD, optimizes the population jointly. It measures the volume occupied by the whole population in a behavioral space instead of relying on pairwise distance updates. That space uses task-agnostic behavioral embeddings, addressing dependence on handcrafted representations. Online learning adjusts how strongly diversity is encouraged during training.

The authors develop both evolutionary and gradient-based versions of the approach. Their results show improved exploration without reduced performance when additional exploration is unnecessary. These findings support treating diversity as a property of the population as a whole and adapting its importance over time. The method therefore addresses both the representation of behavioral variety and its interaction with reward optimization.
neurips-2020-effective-diversity-in-popu.tldr: DvD measures population-wide behavioral diversity and adapts its strength during training, improving exploration in the reported evaluations without sacrificing performance when exploration is unnecessary.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses evaluations of an expensive black-box function sequentially. A choice can matter both for its immediate result and for the later decisions it enables. Common myopic methods focus on the immediate step, while a full lookahead policy requires solving a highly intractable stochastic dynamic program. This paper seeks a computationally practical way to consider several steps ahead.

The approach represents future decisions and possible outcomes in a multi-step scenario tree. This produces nested optimization problems, but the authors avoid solving each nested problem separately. Instead, they optimize all decision variables in the tree jointly through an equivalent one-shot formulation. Efficient multi-step Gaussian process fantasization supplies the imagined future observations used in the lookahead computation.

The authors demonstrate that this combination makes multi-step expected improvement computationally tractable. Across a wide range of benchmarks, it outperforms existing methods. The result shows that a suitable reformulation can make longer-term evaluation planning practical within the studied framework, providing an alternative to choosing each evaluation solely for its immediate expected benefit.
neurips-2020-efficient-nonmyopic-bayesia.tldr: Joint optimization of scenario-tree decisions makes multi-step Bayesian optimization tractable and improves performance across the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Elastic-InfoGAN addresses unsupervised learning of object identity when some classes appear more often than others. The desired representation separates identity from lower-level aspects of an image. The authors first examine InfoGAN’s assumptions about uniformity and demonstrate that these assumptions can prevent it from properly separating object identity in imbalanced data.

The proposed generative model uses identity-preserving transformations of real images as a learning signal. Its key idea is that the discovered discrete factor representing identity should remain invariant under those transformations. This consistency signal helps the model learn an appropriate latent distribution for identity, connecting the representation of identity to the class imbalance present in the data.

Experiments span artificial imbalanced datasets involving MNIST, cars, chairs, and ShapeNet, as well as the real-world YouTube-Faces dataset. The reported results support the method’s ability to isolate object identity as a latent factor. The contribution is an unsupervised approach that uses transformation-based consistency to address the mismatch between a uniformity assumption and unevenly represented identities.
neurips-2020-elastic-infogan-unsupervise.tldr: Elastic-InfoGAN uses identity-preserving transformations to learn an identity representation and latent distribution suited to class-imbalanced data.

paragraphs: Fairness becomes harder when a system contains several decision models. Discrimination in an earlier model can carry forward into later models, so developing each classifier separately cannot guarantee fairness across the system. This paper addresses that interaction by learning multiple classifiers together, with the aim of achieving fairness for all of them simultaneously.

The approach treats each decision model as a soft intervention: a change to how decisions are generated within the system. It then infers the distributions resulting from those interventions and uses them to define both the learning objective and the fairness constraints. This connects the training of individual classifiers to the consequences of decisions elsewhere in the system.

To make the loss and constraints smooth, the authors use surrogate functions. They prove that the resulting excess risk can be bounded in the same mathematical form used for traditional surrogate losses. This supplies theoretical support for their loss formulation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets also support the approach’s effectiveness, complementing the theoretical result with empirical evidence.
neurips-2020-fair-multiple-decision-maki.tldr: The paper jointly learns multiple classifiers using soft interventions to address discrimination that can propagate between decision models.

paragraphs: Branch-and-bound solvers for mixed integer linear programming must repeatedly choose how to branch during search. A graph neural network approach had reduced solver running time, but relied on GPU inference even though the solvers themselves run on CPUs. This paper asks whether that approach remains competitive when practitioners have only a CPU available.

The authors find that the existing GNN approach is not competitive in the CPU-only setting they examine. They propose a hybrid architecture that combines the expressive capabilities of a GNN with computationally inexpensive multilayer perceptrons for branching. The aim is to retain useful predictive power while making the cost of choosing branches suitable for CPU-based solving.

Evaluation covers four classes of mixed integer linear programming problems. The hybrid methods reduce solver running time by up to 26% compared with state-of-the-art methods without a GPU and extrapolate to harder problems than those used for training. The result illustrates why the computational cost of a learned decision rule matters alongside its predictions when it operates inside an optimization solver.
neurips-2020-hybrid-models-for-learning-.tldr: A hybrid GNN–MLP branching model cuts CPU-only solver time by up to 26% in the reported evaluations and generalizes to harder problems.

paragraphs: Symmetries describe transformations associated with invariances, making them valuable building blocks for machine learning. In complex domains such as chemical space, researchers may observe an invariance without being able to write down the transformation responsible for it. This paper approaches the problem inversely: it learns the symmetry transformation from the available information.

The model divides its latent representation into two subspaces. One captures the target, while the other captures the remaining invariant information. Training combines a deep information bottleneck with a regularizer based on continuous mutual information. Minimizing this information quantity is central to the approach because it addresses the relationship between the information stored in the representation’s different parts.

To calculate mutual information in continuous domains, the authors combine correlation matrices with a bijective variable transformation. Experiments on artificial and molecular datasets show better performance than state-of-the-art methods. These results support learning transformations in settings where invariances are observable but an analytical description is unavailable, with the continuous mutual-information treatment serving as a key technical contribution.
neurips-2020-inverse-learning-of-symmetr.tldr: The method learns symmetry transformations through two latent subspaces and continuous mutual-information regularization, outperforming compared methods on artificial and molecular datasets.

paragraphs: An accurate model can still be difficult to use when people cannot understand how its predictions depend on its inputs. This paper proposes an algorithm that produces a continuous, global interpretation of a given continuous black-box function. The aim is an interpretable representation of the function’s behavior as a whole, including the relative importance of features and their interactions.

The algorithm adapts projection pursuit, using Meijer G-functions as its ridge functions in place of the polynomial splines usually used. These functions are differentiable with respect to their parameters. That allows gradient descent to tune the representation, providing the basis for the authors’ claim that the procedure is efficient.

Experiments use five UCI datasets and two machine learning algorithms. The resulting interpretations are reported to be both faithful to the black boxes and parsimonious, using few terms. These findings support the possibility of capturing complicated predictive behavior in a compact continuous representation. The combination matters because an explanation needs both accuracy and manageable complexity to make feature contributions and interactions understandable.
neurips-2020-learning-outside-the-black-.tldr: A projection-pursuit method using trainable Meijer G-functions produces compact, accurate global interpretations of continuous black-box models in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Diplomacy presents reinforcement learning with a combination of challenges: seven players, simultaneous moves, and a large combinatorial action space. Its interactions mix common interests with competition, making the setting more complex than a purely adversarial two-player game. This paper develops methods for learning to play the no-press version through approximate best responses and policy iteration.

The authors introduce an approximate best-response operator designed specifically to handle simultaneous decisions and large combinations of actions. They also develop a family of policy-iteration methods that approximate fictitious play. Together, these components provide a way to improve policies while accounting for the strategic interactions among multiple players.

The resulting agents convincingly outperform the previous state of the art in the reported evaluation. A game-theoretic equilibrium analysis also finds consistent improvements from the new training process. These findings support the use of approximate response computation and iterative policy updates in a setting where action complexity and mixed interests make direct application of simpler reinforcement learning approaches difficult.
neurips-2020-learning-to-play-no-press-d.tldr: Approximate best responses and policy iteration produce stronger no-press Diplomacy agents, with consistent improvements supported by equilibrium analysis.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how a classifier’s architecture influences which features it learns to use. The authors begin with a seemingly simple task: separating distributions that are linearly separable. They find that many advanced convolutional networks struggle depending on the direction of the feature that distinguishes the classes, showing that mathematical separability alone does not make the task equally easy for these networks.

The authors introduce neural anisotropy directions, or NADs, to describe this directional preference. These vectors form an architecture-specific signature that captures which feature directions a network favors when separating inputs. An efficient identification method makes it possible to expose these preferences for several convolutional architectures.

The paper then connects this analysis to CIFAR-10, showing that NADs characterize the features CNNs use to distinguish classes in that dataset. The findings link an architecture’s directional bias to both controlled classification difficulty and feature use on image data. NADs therefore offer a way to describe architectural inductive bias through concrete directions in the input representation.
neurips-2020-neural-anisotropy-direction.tldr: Neural anisotropy directions reveal architecture-specific feature preferences that help explain CNN difficulty on simple tasks and feature use on CIFAR-10.

paragraphs: Learning a directed acyclic graph involves searching a large space of possible structures. Continuous formulations make this search accessible to gradient-based optimization, but a hard requirement that the graph remain acyclic can make optimization difficult. This paper examines the roles of sparsity and acyclicity constraints in linear Gaussian and non-Gaussian models, both asymptotically and with finite samples.

Using its theoretical results, the paper develops a likelihood-based score with soft penalties for sparsity and departures from acyclicity. The authors show that these soft constraints suffice to learn a graph equivalent to the ground-truth DAG in their analysis. Replacing the hard constraint with penalties produces an unconstrained optimization problem that is easier to solve.

The implementation combines gradient-based optimization with GPU acceleration and handles thousands of nodes while maintaining high accuracy. Extensive experiments favor the DAG-penalized likelihood objective over least squares with a hard acyclicity constraint. The findings connect a change in statistical objective and constraint handling to practical scalability, while the stated recovery target remains a graph equivalent to the true structure.
neurips-2020-on-the-role-of-sparsity-and.tldr: A likelihood objective with soft sparsity and acyclicity penalties enables scalable linear DAG learning with recovery of an equivalent graph in the authors’ analysis.

paragraphs: Conditional Value at Risk, or CVaR, is a risk measure that generalizes expectation, recovering it at a boundary parameter setting. It is established in mathematical finance and is gaining interest in machine learning for regularization and fairness. This paper studies the statistical reliability of learning algorithms that minimize CVaR computed from observed training losses.

The central contribution is a PAC-Bayesian generalization bound. It connects optimization of empirical CVaR to a guarantee about performance beyond the training sample, with the bound guaranteed to be small when empirical CVaR is small. This provides theoretical support for the training objective rather than leaving its statistical behavior justified only by observed training performance.

The key technical move reduces CVaR estimation to expectation estimation, allowing tools for the latter problem to address the former. As a further consequence, the authors obtain concentration inequalities for CVaR even for unbounded random variables. The contribution therefore includes both a learning guarantee and an estimation technique useful beyond variables confined to a fixed range.
neurips-2020-pac-bayesian-bound-for-the-.tldr: A reduction from CVaR estimation to expectation estimation yields a PAC-Bayesian generalization bound and concentration results for unbounded variables.

paragraphs: Bayesian learning can require representative samples from a posterior with several isolated modes. Exploring those separated regions is difficult, especially when computation uses noisy mini-batches. This paper proposes a practical sampling method that combines parallel replicas at different temperatures with dynamics designed to handle mini-batch noise.

The replicas evolve in parallel and periodically exchange states. Nosé-Hoover dynamics adaptively neutralizes the noise introduced by mini-batches during their evolution. Exchanges use a newly developed acceptance test that accounts for noise. The authors state that this exchange protocol preserves detailed balance asymptotically, making noise handling part of both the individual dynamics and the coordination between replicas.

Tests on synthetic distributions illustrate the method’s effectiveness for complex multimodal posteriors. Experiments with deep Bayesian neural networks on large-scale datasets report significant improvements over strong baselines. The results support combining temperature-based exploration with adaptive noise control to draw representative samples in the evaluated settings. The asymptotic qualification on detailed balance is part of the method’s stated theoretical characterization.
neurips-2020-replica-exchange-nos-e-hoov.tldr: Temperature-based replica exchanges and noise-adaptive Nosé-Hoover dynamics improve Bayesian sampling from multimodal posteriors in the presence of mini-batch noise.

paragraphs: Patients’ underlying mental states are not directly observed; they must be inferred from measurements such as symptoms and functioning scores. Treatment choice also needs to account for substantial differences between patients. This paper develops an integrated framework that learns latent mental states and individualized treatment recommendations together, drawing information from multiple outcome domains.

The framework follows a psychiatric measurement model in which observed diagnostic measures arise from underlying mental states. It incorporates measurements before and after treatment, along with biological measures, while preserving an invariant structure for representing those states. A multilayer neural network models complex differences in treatment effects between patients.

For a future patient, the policy compares potential mental states under different treatments using that patient’s observed pretreatment measurements. Experiments on simulated data and data from a clinical trial find that the learned policies compare favorably with alternatives for heterogeneous treatment effects and support better outcomes across multiple domains. These results concern the evaluated policies and data, connecting integrated outcome representation to individualized treatment selection.
neurips-2020-representation-learning-for.tldr: An integrated latent-state model combines multiple measurements to learn individualized treatment policies that compare favorably with alternatives in simulation and clinical-trial data.

paragraphs: Hyperbolic spaces can represent hierarchical data using substantially fewer dimensions than ordinary Euclidean spaces. This paper asks whether that representational advantage also benefits classification performed directly in hyperbolic space. It develops theoretical guarantees for learning large-margin classifiers on data with hierarchical structure, extending attention from the embedding itself to the downstream learning task.

The first contribution is a hyperbolic perceptron algorithm with a proof of convergence to a separating hyperplane. The authors then introduce an efficient algorithm for learning a large-margin hyperplane. Its construction carefully injects adversarial examples into learning, using them as part of the procedure for obtaining the desired classifier.

The final theoretical result links classification guarantees to embedding dimension. For hierarchical data that embeds well in hyperbolic space, the lower dimension yields superior guarantees when classification is learned directly there. That condition is central to the result: the advantage is tied to data whose hierarchy has a suitable hyperbolic representation. The paper thus supplies a theoretical connection between compact hierarchical embeddings and subsequent classification.
neurips-2020-robust-large-margin-learnin.tldr: The paper establishes hyperbolic classification guarantees, including large-margin learning and advantages for hierarchical data that embeds well in low-dimensional hyperbolic space.

paragraphs: This paper studies community detection when a graph’s connections reflect both community structure and an additional hidden geometric influence. The community structure follows a stochastic block model, while an unobserved random geometric graph perturbs the connections. The question is whether a spectral method can still identify communities without knowing whether this extra source of structure is present.

The analysis focuses on the second eigenvector of the observed adjacency matrix. The authors identify explicit regimes in which this vector is highly correlated with the true community vector. This connection between an observable matrix quantity and the hidden labels establishes settings where weak or exact community recovery is possible despite the geometric perturbation.

The proof relies on a detailed study of the latent geometric graph’s spectrum, which the authors also present as independently interesting. Understanding that spectrum makes it possible to establish when the community information survives the perturbation. The robustness result is therefore tied to the stated regimes and shows that an algorithm need not explicitly model the hidden geometric graph to succeed there.
neurips-2020-robustness-of-community-det.tldr: The paper identifies regimes where spectral community detection remains effective despite an unobserved random geometric perturbation.

paragraphs: Stein discrepancies help assess whether approximate inference is converging when exact integration and sampling are impractical. Their own computation can nevertheless be expensive because the Stein operator may require evaluating many likelihood terms or potentials. This paper introduces stochastic Stein discrepancies that replace the full operator with subsampled approximations.

The authors prove that these stochastic discrepancies retain the convergence-control properties of standard Stein discrepancies with probability one. This matters because reducing diagnostic cost is useful only if the diagnostic still reliably controls convergence behavior. Along the way, the analysis also establishes convergence of Stein variational gradient descent on unbounded domains, resolving a previously open question.

Experiments cover tuning hyperparameters for biased Markov chain Monte Carlo, selecting approximate MCMC samplers, and stochastic Stein variational gradient descent. Across these applications, stochastic discrepancies deliver comparable inferences with orders of magnitude fewer likelihood evaluations. The contribution combines a theoretical preservation result with evidence that subsampling can substantially reduce the computational cost of inference assessment and related procedures.
neurips-2020-stochastic-stein-discrepanc.tldr: Subsampled Stein discrepancies preserve convergence control with probability one and achieve comparable experimental inferences using far fewer likelihood evaluations.
